subject: Spatially subsampling sites to meet assumption of independence?

messages.author: 1195ce743af3d0d7
messages.subject: Spatially subsampling sites to meet assumption of independence?
parts:
In my data, some of my sites are too close together, and thus likely violate the independence assumption. In order to get around this, I spatially subsample my data to ensure that there is a minimum distance between sites. This procedure is random, and to capture the variability in the subsampling I run the model x number of times with a different random subset of the data. 

Is this a reasonable approach? Are there other papers that address this issue?

If so, I am also wondering how to combine the results from the different model runs. For example, if I run the model x times...I end up with x estimates of all of my model parameters, also with x estimates of their corresponding standard errors. How would I combine these into one estimate for each parameter with one standard error? I can envision three approaches:

1) Brute force: simulate y "raw estimates" for each parameter estimate and standard error, combine these (total n = y * x) and calculate the mean estimate and standard error.
2) Take the mean of the x parameter estimates and the mean of the x standard error estimates
3) Calculate the mean and standard error from the x parameter estimates only (i.e. ignore the standard errors that are estimated within each model run).

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: Spatially subsampling sites to meet assumption of independence?
parts:
Hi Cody,

what are you modeling (e.g., abundance or presence/absence) ? How large are your pixels ? What's the species and what's its movement range ?

I don't think that an ad hoc approach such as yours is necessarily bad, but a more explicit model-based inference framework that directly confronts the nuisance of animal movement among adjacent pixels through movement would be preferrable in my view. Richard Chandler and Andy Royle have that wonderful paper which they hid so well in a journal that no biologists ever reads:
Chandler, R.B. and J.A. Royle. 2013. Spatially-explicit models for inference about density in unmarked or partially marked populations. Annals of Applied Statistics 7:936-954.

In this paper, they describe a spatially explicit Nmix model that exploits that non-independence among adjacent pixels as a source of information about movement and detection.

Then, Ramsey et al. "translated" the Nmix-type of model into an occupancy-type of model here: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jwmg.851/abstract

Perhaps these models could be useful for your problem ?

Best regards ---- Marc

messages.author: 1195ce743af3d0d7
messages.subject: Re: Spatially subsampling sites to meet assumption of independence?
parts:
Hi Marc,

I am using the model described by Dorazio (2014) in which he combines the use of presence-only data with that from planned surveys (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/geb.12216/abstract). In this paper he uses point count data, however I adjusted the model to use detection/non-detection data from camera traps. The planned survey data is modeled following an occupancy model based on a zero-inflated binomial distribution. The model also assumes the species response to the environment is a Poisson point point process. So instead of modeling occupancy, I am modelling intensity (i.e. abundance?). 

The resolution (i.e. grain) of my environmental grids is 1 km x 1 km, and the species of interest is Tapir in Central America. Originally we thought the home range was close to 1 km2, but new data suggests it is probably closer to 10 km2. 

I have just recently discovered the paper by Ramsey that you mentioned, and applied it to some of my data in order to compare the results with the Dorazio model from above. I did have some problems with convergence for most of the data I used, but the models that did converge seemed interesting. I have data from several different researchers and survey efforts, and some of those surveys have the right amount of data to run the Ramsey model, while others don't (enough sites and detections, the right distance between them).

Ideally I would like to combine some of the ideas from the two frameworks (Dorazio's and Ramsey's), as they both have advantages, but figuring out how to do that is probably above my abilities. Additional next steps might also include adopting a spatio-temporal framework.  Right now I take a static approach, despite the fact that I have about a decade worth of data.

In the meantime, I'm focusing on the application of Dorazio's model.  

Thanks again. If you have any thoughts about which of the three ad hoc approaches I mentioned seems most appropriate, let me know. 

By the way, your AHM book is awesome!

messages.author: d647e6438dc3aad6
messages.subject: Re: Spatially subsampling sites to meet assumption of independence?
parts:
Hi Cody,

It might be worth looking into an approach called Generalized Random Tessellation Stratified (GRTS) sampling. (The method is easier to digest than the name!) GRTS sampling is meant to guide sampling design, but I think it could work for you here. The GRTS sampling process produces a ranked list of spatially balanced sites. Normally one would start sampling from the top of the list to achieve a balanced sample. However, data from any or all sites on the list can be used when weighted according to the GRTS draw. The resulting weighted sample will be spatially balanced, even if you include all your sites, so there is no need to worry about how close together the points are. A site that is very close to another site would simply be down-weighted relative to the other, more distant sites. I have only just started using GRTS but it seems to be an excellent way to achieve a spatially balanced sample and eliminate the concern about spatial autocorrelation in the analysis. Of course it's possible that others' suggestions might be more relevant for your particular study, or easier to implement for your dataset, but I thought I'd mention it.

The best overview of the method that I've found is in this chapter:

Olsen AR, Kincaid TM, Q P (2012) Spatially balanced survey designs for natural resources. In: Gitzen RA, Millspaugh JJ, Cooper AB, Licht DS (eds) Design and Analysis of Long-term Ecological Monitoring Studies. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, United Kingdom and New York, NY, USA, pp 126–150

The chapter is in the public domain in the U.S. (federal employee as author) and I believe my electronic copy came from Research Gate. Feel free to contact me off-list if you have trouble finding a copy and want to pursue GRTS.

Another good overview is:

Stevens DL, Olsen AR (2004) Spatially balanced sampling of natural resources. J Am Stat Assoc 99:262–278.

and several other Stevens & Olsen papers are relevant, but I found the book chapter to be the clearest and easiest to read.

There is also an R package that implements GRTS: "spsurvey".


For your second question: Have you considered a model-averaging approach?

Cheers,

Emily
